source_text: Quatenus autem et de scripturis adversus veritatem argumentari consuetudo est, statim opponitur nobis nullam mentionem virginum ab apostolo factam ubi de velamine praefinit, sed tantum mulieres nominatas, cum, si voluisset et virgines tegi, de virginibus quoque cum mulieribus nominatis pronuntiasset: quomodo illic, inquit, ubi de nuptiis tractat, quid observandum sit (??)tiam de virginibus declarat. Itaque non contineri eas lega velandi capitis, ut non nominatas in hac lege, immo ex hoc revelari, qua non i(??)beutur quae nec nominantur. Sed et nos eandem argumentationem retorquemus. Qui enim sciebat alias utriusque generis facere mentionem, virginis dico et mulieris, id est non virginis, ex ca(??) distinctionis, in his, in quibus non nominat virginem, non facie(??)s distinctionem ostendit condicionis communionem. Ceterum potu hic quoque constituere differentiam inter virginem et mulierem, sicut alibi dicit, Divisa est mulier et virgo. Igitur quas non divisit tacendo, in(??)teravit. Nec tamen quia illic divisa est et mulier et virgo, hic quoque patrocinabitur illa divisio, ut quidam vo(??)t. Quanta enim alibi dicta non valent, ubi dicta scilicet non sunt, nisi si eadem sit causa quae alibi, ut sufficiat semel dictum? Illa autem causa virginis et mulieris longe divisa est ab hac specie. Divisa est, inquit, mulier et virgo. Quare? quoniam innupta, id est virgo, cogitat ea quae sunt domini, ut sit sancta et corpore et spiritu, nupta autem, id est non virgo, cogitat quomodo plac(??) viro. Haec erit interpretatio divisionis illius, nullum habens lec(??) in isto capitu(??)o, in quo neque de nuptiis neque de animo et cogitatu mulieris et virginis pronuntiatum, sed de capite velande. Cuius nullam volens esse disceptationem spiritus sanctus uno nomine mulieris etiam virginem intellegi voluit, quam proprie (??) nominando a muliere non separavit, et non separando coniunxit ei a qua non separavit. Novum est nunc ergo principali vocabulo uti et cetera nihilominus in eo vocabulo intellegi, ubi nulla est necessitas singillatim distinguendae universitatis? Naturaliter compendium sermonis et gratum et necessarium est, quoniam sermo laciniosus et onerosus et vanus est. Sic et generalibus vocabulis contenti sumus, comprehendentibus in se specialium intellectum. Ergo iam de vocabulo ipso. Naturale vocabulum est femina. Naturalis vocabuli generale mulier. Generalis etiam speciale virgo vel nupta vel vidua vel quot etiam aetatis nomina accedunt. Subiectum igitur est generali speciale, quia generale prius est, et subcessivum antecessivo et portionale universali; in ipso intellegitur cui subicitur, et in ipso significatur, quia in ipso continetur. Sic nec manus nec pes nec ullum membrorum desiderat significari corpore nominato. Et si mundum dixeris, illic erit et caelum et quae in eo, sol et luna et sidera et astra et terra et freta et ominis census elementorum. Omnia dixeris, cum id dixeris quod ex omnibus constat. Sic et mulierem nominando quicquid est mulieris nominavit.
orientation: Tertullian answers the objection that the apostle ordered only women and not virgins to wear the veil.
pass_a_gloss: In as much as it is also custom to argue from Scriptures against truth, at once there is objected to us that no mention of virgins was made by the apostle where he lays down beforehand about the veil, but only women were named, since, if he had wished also virgins to be veiled, he would have pronounced about virgins also when women were named: as there, he says, where he treats about marriages, what must be observed ... he declares also about virgins. Therefore they are not held by the law of veiling the head, as not named in this law, but rather from this they are unveiled, because the things which are not even named are not commanded. But also we hurl back the same argumentation. For he who knew elsewhere to make mention of each kind, of virgin I mean and of woman, that is not virgin, from cause of distinction, in those matters in which he does not name virgin, by not making distinction he shows sharing of condition. For the rest he could have established here also a difference between virgin and woman, just as elsewhere he says, Divided is woman and virgin. Therefore those whom he did not divide by being silent, he ... [text damaged]. Nor yet because there both woman and virgin was divided, will that division give support here also, as some wish. For how much force do things said elsewhere not have, where that is they were not said, unless the cause be the same as elsewhere, so that a thing once said suffices? But that cause of virgin and of woman is far divided from this case. Divided is, he says, woman and virgin. For what reason? Since the unwedded woman, that is virgin, thinks the things which are of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit, but the wedded woman, that is not virgin, thinks how she may please man. This will be the interpretation of that division, having no place in this chapter, in which neither about marriages nor about the mind and thought of woman and of virgin was pronounced, but about head to be veiled. Of which head, willing there to be no dispute, the holy spirit willed virgin also to be understood by the one name of woman, whom by properly ... by naming he did not separate from woman, and by not separating he joined her to her from whom he did not separate. Is it then now a new thing to use the chief word and nevertheless the rest to be understood in that word, where there is no need of distinguishing the whole one by one? Naturally a shortening of speech is both pleasing and necessary, since wordy speech is both burdensome and empty. So also we are content with general words, comprehending in themselves the understanding of special things. Therefore now about the word itself. Female is a natural word. Woman is the general of the natural word. Of the general also the special is virgin or bride or widow or however many names of age also come to them. The special therefore is subjected to the general, because the general is prior, and the subsequent to the antecedent and the partial to the universal; in the general itself is understood that which is subjected to it, and in the general itself it is signified, because in the general itself it is contained. So neither hand nor foot nor any of the limbs needs to be signified when the body has been named. And if you will have said world, there will be both heaven and the things which are in it, sun and moon and stars and constellations and earth and seas and every reckoning of the elements. You will have said all things, when you will have said that which consists from all things. So also by naming woman he named whatever is of woman.

choices.why: brief glossary requires woman for the general term including virgins
keeps legal force of lex and glossary veil and head
literal order preserves the distinction Tertullian is arguing about
literal sense that silence shows one shared standing, not two rules
stresses one general word covering virgin, central to argument

pass_b_english: Custom argues from Scripture against truth, as it always does. Our opponents meet us at once with this objection. They say the apostle makes no mention of virgins where he lays down the veil. He names only women. If he had wanted virgins to be veiled, they say, he would have spoken of virgins by name alongside women. He does just that elsewhere. Where he treats marriage, he also declares what virgins must observe.

So they claim virgins are not held by the law of veiling the head. The law does not name them, so it does not command them. Indeed, they say, this leaves them unveiled, since those who are not even named are not commanded. We turn the same argument back on them. The apostle knew how to name each kind separately elsewhere, virgin and woman, that is, a woman who is not a virgin. He drew that distinction when he needed it. Where he does not name the virgin, he drops the distinction on purpose. His silence proves sharing of condition. He could have set virgin apart from woman here as well.

He says elsewhere, "Woman and virgin are divided." So those he did not divide by his silence, he joined. Some think that division helps them here. It does not. What is said elsewhere has no force where it is not said, unless the cause is the same elsewhere, so that saying it once is enough. But the cause that divides virgin and woman there lies far from this case. The apostle says, "The unmarried — that is, the virgin — cares for the things of the Lord, so she may be holy in body and in spirit, but the married — that is, a woman who is not a virgin — cares how to please her husband" (1 Corinthians 7:34). That explains the division there. It has no place in this chapter. Here he pronounces nothing about marriage, nor about the mind and thoughts of woman and virgin. He speaks only about veiling the head. The Holy Spirit wanted no dispute about this. He willed the virgin to be understood under the one name of woman. He did not separate her by naming her apart from woman, and by not separating her he joined her to the woman from whom he did not separate her.

Is it strange now to use the leading word and still mean all the rest under that word, when there is no need to spell out each part of the whole? Short speech is both welcome and needed by nature. Long, wordy speech is burdensome and empty. So we rest content with general words, which hold the lesser kinds inside themselves. Take the word itself. Female is the word of nature. Woman is the general form of that word of nature. Under that general term come the special terms, virgin or married or widow, with as many names of age as join them. The special rests under the general, for the general comes first, the later follows the earlier, and the part belongs to the whole. What is subject to it is understood in it and meant in it, because it is held in it. When you name the body, you need not name each limb, neither hand nor foot nor any other part. If you say world, heaven is there with all it holds, sun and moon and stars, earth and seas, and every kind of element. You have named them all when you name what holds them all. So in naming woman he has named whatever belongs to woman.

problems.quote: Their going unveiled, they say, proves it.
problems.source_quote: immo ex hoc revelari, qua non i(??)beutur quae nec nominantur
problems.why: Source says they are rather unveiled from this, since those not named are not commanded; English turns it into a proof from practice and loses the reasoning.
problems.fix: Indeed, they say, virgins are left unveiled by this, since those who are not even named are not commanded.

problems.quote: He says elsewhere, "Woman and virgin are divided." Some think that division helps them here.
problems.source_quote: Igitur quas non divisit tacendo, coniunxit.
problems.why: The retort that silence joins those he did not divide is missing between the quotation and the opponents' appeal.
problems.fix: So those he did not divide by his silence, he joined. Some think that division helps them here.
problems.ruling: Source 'Igitur quas non divisit tacendo, in(??)teravit' (conjoined/joined) is a distinct step in the argument; English omits it entirely between quotation and 'Some think'.

last_rejected.quote: where he lays down the veil
last_rejected.why: praefinit de velamine means he prescribes the rule about the veil. "Lays down the veil" reads as setting the veil aside.
last_rejected.fix: where he lays down the rule about the veil
last_rejected.ruling: "lays down the veil" is idiomatic for laying down a rule about the veil; praefinit de velamine = 'prescribes concerning the veil'. Not a plausible reading as setting aside.

last_rejected.quote: The unmarried — that is, the virgin — cares for the things of the Lord, so she may be holy in body and in spirit, but the married — that is, a woman who is not a virgin — cares how to please her husband
last_rejected.source_quote: innupta, id est virgo, cogitat ea quae sunt domini, ut sit sancta et corpore et spiritu, nupta autem, id est non virgo, cogitat quomodo plac(??) viro
last_rejected.why: The id est glosses are Tertullian's, but they sit inside the apostle's quotation and the 1 Corinthians 7:34 citation.
last_rejected.fix: The unmarried woman cares for the things of the Lord, so she may be holy in body and in spirit, but the married woman cares how to please her husband. That is, the virgin and the woman who is not a virgin.
last_rejected.ruling: The id est glosses are Tertullian's interjected within the quoted text, but the English reads as his explanatory glosses and 7:34 cite is accurate; reader not materially misled.
